units.passage: Using your ideas from Step 3 above, explain to your students the reasons that you do or don’t want them to use AI as they develop the skills you want them to learn. units.passage: Ask students to read your policy and then write down two things they find helpful and two genuine questions they have about your policy. Have students share these reactions in small groups and reach consensus on what they find helpful and what questions they’d like to discuss. Have groups share out and then make time for a whole class discussion.
units.why: Conversation plan 1: "Ask students to read your policy and then write down two things they find helpful and two genuine questions" is a concrete way to discuss the rules, P66.

units.passage: If you don’t want students to use AI, it is important that you give them an opportunity to consider how doing work without artificial intelligence will help them learn and grow. Alternately, if you do want students to use AI, students also need to articulate how using artificial intelligence will support their learning.
units.why: Conversation plan 2: "it is important that you give them an opportunity to consider how doing work without artificial intelligence will help them learn" asks instructors who ban AI to let students weigh the reasons; P66.

units.passage: You may want to explore the uses and limitations of AI with your students. This is often best done by having students do some analytic work. For example, you could ask students to evaluate two short arguments, one generated by AI and one by a person. Do not reveal that one argument was AI-generated. Students’ evaluations will allow you and them to uncover some of the problems with arguments generated by AI. If you want students to explore what AI does well, have them analyze AI-generated work and consider how it could support their work.
units.why: Conversation plan 3: "You may want to explore the uses and limitations of AI with your students" by comparing AI and human arguments; a class discussion of AI (P66), closest type, though it also teaches AI limits.
units.fit_note: Teaching about AI limitations through an in-class analytic activity, not just explaining a rule. | P66 is explaining rules and discussing AI; this unit specifically suggests classroom analysis of AI's limitations.

units.passage: With both these approaches, students perceive these writing assignments as lower-stakes assignments, feel supported by the instructor, and see assessment as a way to learn rather than a performance that might sink their grade. units.why: Sample statement: 'We will also discuss the role of AI in writing processes', the instructor commits to discuss AI in class, P66.

units.passage: Instructor Tip: Discuss AI policies early in the semester, include an “AI use” section on all assignment instructions, and provide examples of acceptable and unacceptable use in your course.
units.why: 'Discuss AI policies early in the semester' and give examples goes beyond listing the rule, so P66; the 'AI use' section on assignments is noted.
units.fit_note: Also recommends an 'AI use' section on all assignment instructions (P09).

units.passage: Be transparent and address the topic upfront with students.
units.why: "Be transparent and address the topic upfront with students" asks instructors to talk about AI with students at the start; P66 (explain and discuss) fits better than P09 because it is about addressing the topic, not a syllabus statement.

units.passage: In Class: Instructors should begin their course with a verbal explanation of their expectations, including when and how AI use will be appropriate
units.why: "Instructors should begin their course with a verbal explanation of their expectations, including when and how AI use will be appropriate" asks for oral explanation at course start; explaining and discussing the rules is P66.
units.fit_note: The rule is to state expectations orally; it does not require giving reasons.

units.passage: They should encourage students to share their perspectives and ask questions and revisit AI usage expectations at the start of new assignments throughout the semester
units.why: "encourage students to share their perspectives and ask questions and revisit AI usage expectations at the start of new assignments" invites discussion and repeats expectations, P66.

units.passage: Explain the reasoning behind your policy and its implications.
units.why: "Explain the reasoning behind your policy and its implications" asks instructors to give students reasons (P66).

units.passage: Discuss your policy in multiple places, at multiple times, and in multiple ways.
units.why: "Discuss your policy in multiple places, at multiple times, and in multiple ways" is about communicating expectations repeatedly (P66, going beyond listing the rule).

units.passage: Discuss with your students verbally at the beginning of a course and also during relevant portions of the course.
units.why: "Discuss with your students verbally at the beginning of a course and also during relevant portions of the course" is class discussion of the rules (P66).

units.passage: Use plain, direct, and accurate language during generative AI discussions.
units.why: "Use plain, direct, and accurate language during generative AI discussions" concerns wording of the rules (P66).

units.passage: Use conversations about Generative AI as a starting point to talk about the ethics of these tools and the larger ethical dimensions. Explain the value of what you're teaching to your students and the value of them learning it for themselves.
units.why: Conversations should be "a starting point to talk about the ethics of these tools" and explain the value of learning the material oneself (P66, reasons given to students).
units.fit_note: Also stresses the learning-value rationale (P41) and treats AI ethics as a conversation starter.

units.passage: Don't be afraid to discuss the gray areas with your students. Involve them in ongoing conversations as we progress using these new technologies.
units.why: "Don't be afraid to discuss the gray areas with your students" invites open discussion of the rules (P66).

units.passage: Let students know that while there are appropriate uses for genAI, there are also inappropriate and unethical uses, and share with them concerns about bias and intellectual property rights.
units.why: 'Let students know that while there are appropriate uses for genAI, there are also inappropriate and unethical uses' tells instructors to explain where lines fall (P66).

units.passage: Responsible Use Scenarios for GenAI. These scenarios can be used with students as an activity or to generate discussions on the appropriate use of GenAI.
units.why: The "Responsible Use Scenarios" can be used with students "as an activity or to generate discussions", a classroom discussion tool (P66).

units.passage: Instead of relying on detection software alone, instructors should focus on promoting transparency and critical engagement with GenAI tools in their courses.
units.why: Instructors "should focus on promoting transparency and critical engagement" with students instead of detection, going beyond listing rules, P66.
units.fit_note: Offered as an alternative to detection.

units.passage: Explain your GenAI policy and rationale clearly.
units.why: "Explain your GenAI policy and rationale clearly" is under Instructor Recommendations and does not push AI use (A encourage, B neutral). Neutral.

units.passage: Encourage discussion about GenAI use and limits.
units.why: "Encourage discussion about GenAI use and limits" is discussing AI in class, P66.

units.passage: Provide examples of appropriate vs. inappropriate uses.
units.why: "Provide examples of appropriate vs. inappropriate uses" is a recommendation about communicating, not a stance on AI use (A encourage, B neutral). Neutral.
units.fit_note: Concrete examples to clarify the rule.

units.passage: Going beyond the syllabus statement when it comes to ethics and artificial intelligence can be beneficial. At the beginning of your course, discussing the implications of AI misuse in the subject and potential career fields relating to the course can help students learn about the importance of submitting their own work and properly attributing resources, including technology
units.policy: Faculty discuss the implications of AI misuse in the subject and in potential career fields at the beginning of the course, going beyond the syllabus statement.
units.why: The guide recommends discussing 'the implications of AI misuse in the subject and potential career fields' at the start of the course, going beyond the syllabus. Explaining and discussing AI rules with students is exactly P66; it is timed at course start and uses 'can be beneficial', hence 'should'.
